name: Fire Drawing Workshop
description:
Have you ever played with fire? 
In this hands-on workshop participants learn a technique the artist has spent five years developing: burning or “fuming” wood with matches, candles, and pyrography tools to create textured, tonal, almost painterly images. The process allows partial control over the outcome, producing fine relief-like details and layered effects akin to glazing with flame. 
Fire is at the heart of creation, alongside wood and the artist’s own hands, in a slow, attentive dialogue between intention and element. Participants will experiment directly with flame and wood, exploring a completely new material language while reconnecting with something older: attentiveness to matter, to process, and to the natural world. 
Please Note: Limited to 50 seats. Children 6+ are welcome to attend, provided they are accompanied by a parent or caregiver.

name: Swar, Soch, Laya
description:
Music begins where words end. 
This evening of Hindustani classical music explores the intimate connection between thought, emotion and musical expression. Through vocals and tabla, the unspoken nuances of the inner mind are expressed through raga, swara, alaap and laya. 
The evening features a vocal recital by Mandakini, exploring the depth, beauty and emotional dimensions of the raga through meditative expanse and rhythmic interplay. It also features a solo tabla presentation by Kaustuv, showcasing the expressive vocabulary of tabla in the traditional progression of Peshkar, Kayda, Rela, Gat and Tukda. Through rhythm, composition and improvisation, the two presentations create an evening where thought becomes swara, silence becomes sound, and rhythm becomes expression.

name: Leading Climate Action from the Ground Up
description:
Who decides how to run the Western Ghats? 
This panel discussion examines the emerging frames in climate communication, and the public outcry they generate. Specifically, the policy imbroglio over declaring the Western Ghats a World Heritage Site, which is yet to reach a decisive point. Through case studies of Kodagu and Chikmagalur, two economically rich districts of Karnataka, the discussion examines community and citizen activism, alongside the role and impact of social media. 
The Central Government has recently reissued its draft notification proposing an Ecologically Sensitive Zone across the Western Ghats, after the previous draft lapsed amid continuing differences between the six states it traverses. Ambiguity in policy and legislation can lead to skewed development, often at the cost of fragile biodiversity and the communities that depend on it. The discussion also outlines the essential role offline, on-ground efforts play in mediating policy, legislation and community action.

name: Lure of the Monsoon
description:
Images of clouds gathering low, the patter of rain on parched earth, the scent that rises when the first drops fall: the monsoon is far more than a change in season. It is a mood, a memory, a music that has moved through centuries of ragas, waiting to be heard again. 
This concert is a celebration of the intimate relationship between Hindustani classical music and the Indian monsoon, illustrating how the atmosphere of rain transforms into melody. For centuries, the arrival of the rains has inspired musicians, poets, and artists, giving rise to a rich repertoire of ragas that evoke the anticipation of gathering clouds, the freshness of the first showers, and the quiet romance of the season. What does the monsoon sound like, if you listen closely enough?

name: The Many Pasts of Panipat, 1761
description:
A great “what if?” moment in Indian history, the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 has produced martyrs, ballads, and endless partisan debate. This lecture examines how its retelling, across school textbooks, Hindu nationalist historiography, and cinema, has flattened a complex event into a tale of heroes and villains. It raises the question, whose Panipat are we really remembering? 
The vernacular primary sources tell a different story: where popular memory insists on certainty, they equivocate, contradict, and complicate. A micro history of the battle reveals multiple pasts, remembered and recorded by multiple men. This lecture makes a case for why critical historians cannot ignore this plurality while narrating the event to a generation raised on a communal rendering of Indian history. 
About Satish Chandra 
Professor Satish Chandra (1922-2017) was one of India’s foremost historians and a towering authority on medieval Indian history. Over a distinguished four-decade career, he taught at leading universities across the country, including Allahabad University, Aligarh Muslim University, Delhi University, Rajasthan University, and finally Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). At JNU, he co-founded the Centre for Historical Studies alongside S. Gopal, Bipin Chandra, and Romila Thapar. As Chairman of the University Grants Commission, he went on to help shape academic life across India, and in 1985, deeply committed to intellectual exchange, he co-founded the Society for Indian Ocean Studies. A thoughtful historian who brought a Marxist approach to the field, Chandra’s work bridged eras and ideas, leaving an enduring mark on the study of India’s past.

name: Mystik Vibes
description:
Mystik Vibes is an Indo-Jazz musical journey by Amith Nadig, Muthu Kumar, and Aman Mahajan, a meeting point where the melodic language of Carnatic and Hindustani music finds kinship with the freedom of Jazz. Beneath three distinct traditions, the musicians uncover a single, shared pulse: improvisation, emotion, breath. If music can dissolve the boundaries between such different worlds, what else might dissolve, if we listened closely enough? 
Built almost entirely from original compositions, each piece carries the story of the musician who wrote it, and the friendship between all three. Every note becomes a small act of translation, one tradition speaking to another, until the differences soften and only the music remains. A short Q&A follows the performance, encouraging audiences to engage deeply with the experience.

name: In Search of Home
description:
Lucknow is no longer quite the city it once was: a place of old-world grace, Urdu poetry, and tehzeeb, now reshaped by market capitalism and communalism. This conversation, centred on the novella Homecoming, explores what it means for India to undergo one of the largest urbanisations in history. With cities and culture morphing into unrecognisable, and sometimes alienating, new forms, what makes a space worth belonging to? 
Beyond the novel lies a larger question of language tied to belonging: how lived experience is shaped by the language spoken in a place, a thread the author has long explored. The conversation will also examine the exchange between author and reader, asking what spaces writing can leave for imagination to fill.

name: Tiger Man, Burning Bright!
description:
Can the recovery of a single species hold the key to saving creatures across an entire continent? 
Based on Tiger Memories: My Life in Wildlife Conservation by K. Ullas Karanth, this panel discussion traces the history and social context of tiger conservation in India and Asia over the past six decades. The conversation illustrates the centrality of rigorous wildlife science to effective conservation, combining top-down and bottom-up approaches from field biology and statistical ecology, and explores the future prospects for tigers and wild nature in a wider socio-environmental context. 
Coauthored with naturalist Joshua Mathew and published by Penguin Random House India, the book illustrates Karanth’s wildlife adventures, pioneering research, and passionate battles to save big cats and wild nature. It traces his long career studying and conserving wild tigers, from exploring the forests of Karnataka’s Malenad as a teenager to becoming one of the world’s leading wildlife biologists.

name: India after Bhagat Singh
description:
Language: Hindi, Urdu, and English 
What happened to the fierce romanticism of Bhagat Singh’s revolutionary spirit? 
This solo play explores the profound changes the nation has undergone since the martyrdom of the legendary freedom fighter. Breathing new life into his revolutionary philosophy, the performance holds his core ideals of justice, equality, and freedom, up against modern-day socio-political scenarios. 
The soil of Jallianwala Bagh, the site of the massacre that revolutionised young Bhagat Singh, is not merely dirt preserved in an urn. It is a witness to systemic cruelty, unheeded cries, and human sacrifice. When destruction and violence unfold today, in Manipur, Kashmir, or the Hasdeo forests, the same soil bleeds again. The play asks: how many unrecognised Jallianwala Baghs must exist before humanity notices? Both a mirror to contemporary society and an urgent call to remember the true spirit of the nation’s struggle, this performance refuses to let history stay history.

name: Reading Allama with D.R. Nagaraj
description:
Language: Kannada and English 
What does it mean to search for the divine at the very limits of language itself? 
This event centres on the English translation of D.R. Nagaraj’s final and most innovative work: an engagement with the twelfth-century Shaiva mystic and poet, Allama Prabhu. The session opens with an introduction to Allama and his enigmatic vachanas, moves into a reflection on the work of translating into English the nuanced thought of Nagaraj, and arrives at a conversation on what it takes to carry a difficult, vital inheritance across language and time. 
Nagaraj situates Allama across three widening contexts: medieval Shaiva philosophy, the pan-Indian bhakti movement, and Indian mystical thought more broadly, reading him alongside poet-spiritualists like Basava, the philosopher Abhinavagupta, and Gorakhnath. Central to this vision is Allama’s resistance to Sringara, the erotic and romantic mode typical of devotional poetry, pushing instead toward a bhakti that exceeds expression altogether. In tracing Allama’s thought, the discussion is equally a tribute to Nagaraj himself, whose singular scholarly imagination made this reading possible, and whose legacy now finds new life in a new language, for new audiences.

name: Enchantment
description:
Shaped by Pandit Ravi Shankar’s own witty and poignant words, Enchantment is a theatrical journey into the mind of the sitar maestro, weaving theatre, live dance and music into a richly immersive experience. Instead of a standard retelling of the global icon’s legendary career, this bioplay steps into the inner world of his doubts, regrets, struggles, and the fiery resolve that carried him from a boy dancer in Paris to one of the most influential musicians of the 20th century. Through moments of vulnerability and brilliance, the play reveals how Ravi Shankar transformed adversity into artistic triumph. 
The journey passes through the four stages in his life: 

the boy in Paris, acclaimed as a dancer in his brother’s troupe
the disciple undergoing relentless training in music in a remote Indian town
the zealous artist struggling to establish a career
the global icon, putting Indian music on the world map.

Written and directed by Gowri Ramnarayan, the production features Ravi Shankar’s original sitar recordings, and also some of his own compositions, rendered exclusively for Enchantment by lead vocalist Bombay Jayashri, with Aditya Prakash and Vignesh Ishwar. Premiered in Chennai in September 2025, this widely acclaimed play has just completed a coast-to-coast US Tour with 15 shows. 
Director’s Note
 
Every play begins with a question. Enchantment asks – how do you conjure up a legendary artist of your own times on the stage, whose life has been exhaustively documented on page and screen? 
Only if I relied on personal interactions over the years with the maestro, and his partner of 24 years, Kamala Chakravarti, and my interviews with him as a journalist. I had to focus on the protagonist’s doubts and regrets to transform biography into the universal human struggle to survive, to succeed. I could use dance, and the maestro’s own
music to convey what words cannot express. 
Two actors. Two dancers. A lighting person. They actualise an entire life story. The stage showcases a superstar. But audiences see a human being whose vulnerabilities are their own.

name: Shera
description:
20 min | Kumaoni with English subtitles 
All Monu can think about as he roams the forests with his best friend Raju, is spotting the elusive leopard, Shera, before his family moves away to the city. Time is running out, so Raju comes up with an idea: a little dangerous, but maybe just crazy enough to work. Will they find Shera in time? 
Watch the film, flip through the beautifully illustrated graphic book, and meet the storyteller behind it all! Shera began as a short film and grew into a graphic book, hand-painted by acclaimed artist Allen Shaw, bringing to life the magic and mystery of the Himalayan valleys of Kumaon. Beyond the adventure lies a story about home, moving away, and a community learning to share its world with a wild, wonderful neighbour. 

Around the World in 50 Sundays is a journey that begins, not with a ticket, but with opening a book. In a city like Bangalore where families are always in motion, the BIC Library hopes to offer stillness and a quiet, welcoming space for both parents and children where reading becomes a shared experience. Every Sunday, we open our doors to invite you into a library that listens; building a rhythm of return, a habit of joy and a new community bound not just by books, but by the weekly ritual of reading together.

name: The Story We Think We Know
description:
The Undocumented is a work of narrative non-fiction that follows a Bangladeshi family who crossed into India without papers in 2009, and the life they built since. This conversation, based on the book, explore migration: why people leave, what they encounter on arrival, and what it means to build a life where your presence can be questioned. The panel will also discuss the invisible work of telling someone else’s story. 
Amid love, survival, loss, and the constant uncertainty of being undocumented, the book looks past the labels to uncover the lives underneath; beyond the politics of migration to the histories, routines, and relationships that make a place home.
